title: Pareus' four senses of immortality: unfallen Adam's was the power of not dying, given union with a perfect soul
source_text: XXI. Et similiter Pareus immortalitatem illam, qua homo ante peccatum corpore immortalis erat, dicit fuisse potentiam non moriendi, seu negationem actus moriendi, ex hypothesi unionis cum anima originaliter perfecta, licet corpus hominis esset in se mortale. Immortalitas, inquit, significat primo impotentiam moriendi absolutam & natura. Sic solus Deus immortalitatem habet. Sic Patres negant, & nos negamus hominem immortalem fuisse natura. Secundo impotentiam moriendi ex gratia creationis: Sic Angeli, animae humanae sunt immortales. Tertio impotentiam moriendi ex gratia doni: sic corpora beatorum immortalitatem habebunt. Quarto potentiam non moriendi, seu negationem actus moriendi, ex aliqua hypothesi, licet in se sit mortale. Sic homo ante peccatum immortalis erat corpore, ex hypothesi unionis cum anima originaliter perfecta, immortali. In lib. adversus Bell. de Grat. primi hominis, cap. 9.
pass_a_gloss: And similarly Pareus says that that immortality, by which man before sin was immortal in body, was the power of not dying, or the negation of the act of dying, on the hypothesis of union with a soul originally perfect, although the body of man was in itself mortal. Immortality, he says, signifies first the impotence of dying absolute and by nature. So God alone has immortality. So the Fathers deny, and we deny, that man was immortal by nature. Second the impotence of dying from the grace of creation: So Angels, human souls are immortal. Third the impotence of dying from the grace of gift: so the bodies of the blessed will have immortality. Fourth the power of not dying, or the negation of the act of dying, from some hypothesis, although in itself it be mortal. So man before sin was immortal in body, on the hypothesis of union with an immortal soul originally perfect. In the book against Bellarmine on the Grace of the first man, chapter 9.
pass_b_english: Pareus likewise says that the immortality by which man before sin was immortal in body was a power of not dying, that is, the absence of the act of dying, on the supposition of its union with a soul perfect from its origin, although man's body was mortal in itself.

"Immortality," he says, "means first an inability to die that is absolute and by nature. In this sense God alone has immortality, and in this sense the Fathers deny, and we deny, that man was immortal by nature. Second, an inability to die by the grace of creation: so angels and human souls are immortal. Third, an inability to die by the grace of a gift: so the bodies of the blessed will have immortality. Fourth, a power of not dying, that is, the absence of the act of dying, on some supposition, though the thing is mortal in itself. In this sense man before sin was immortal in body, on the supposition of its union with an immortal soul perfect from its origin." (Pareus, against Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9.)

choices.english: the absence of the act of dying
choices.why: Scholastic 'negatio' is absence, not denial; the English avoids implying a refusal.
